r: The applied work is a student mapping business career options to personal skills, drafting a professional-growth plan, learning the job-search process, and building a professional network. Mapped to O*NET, this is Getting Information, Organizing and Planning work, and Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships. Resume drafting, occupational research, and job-posting triage are genuinely exposed: observed-usage data shows writing and office tasks are a prominent share of AI activity, and models draft cover letters and career summaries competently. But the course's core is the student's own self-assessment and live networking, real-time interpersonal work task-exposure research places among low-exposure categories. There is no licensure lock, only AACSB, a weak brake. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact: AI assists the paperwork, but it does not build the student's networking relationships or self-knowledge. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI career agents will retrieve postings, tailor application materials, and run mock interviews fluently, automating most of the job-search execution this one-credit course introduces. The instrumental case erodes at the edges as the research-and-drafting shell is increasingly AI-performed. But the durable residue is embodied and personal: cultivating a real professional network and forming an honest self-assessment are interpersonal, presence-based activities that resist substitution, and the productivity evidence shows AI augments rather than replaces relational work. No accreditation or licensure gates this course, so nothing external holds it in place, yet nothing external is needed because the competence is the student's own career agency. The rating stays Low, with the hedge that course time plausibly shifts toward networking and self-reflection as AI absorbs the mechanical search tasks.

A decade out, AI will handle nearly all mechanical job-search work: discovery, matching, materials, and scheduling, and could coach interview practice convincingly. The honest uncertainty is whether a dedicated career-management course still adds instrumental value when tools do the legwork. But the central case still has students needing to build genuine professional relationships and to know their own aptitudes and goals, tasks task-exposure research keeps outside AI's automatable range because they are interpersonal and self-referential. Diffusion and adoption lag capability, and career self-management is inherently the student's to perform. The rating holds Low, capped not by any institutional mandate but by the embodied, personal nature of networking and self-assessment. The caveat is real: if the course narrowed to only the automatable search mechanics, its instrumental case would weaken more than this rating implies.
BUS 1500.d: The purpose of this course is to help students explore business career opportunities, match job requirements to personal skills and abilities, develop a plan for professional growth, and introduce students to the job search process. Students will gain an understanding of the value and the process of building a professional network.

r: The course transmits foundational business concepts (management, marketing, finance, operations, and contemporary issues) to give majors context and non-majors literacy. Mapped to O*NET, the applied work is Getting Information, Analyzing Data or Information, and Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others: explaining how business functions interrelate and summarizing current issues. This informational, explanatory content is squarely exposed; observed-usage data shows business and office tasks are a prominent, growing share of AI use, and models explain business concepts fluently. Crucially, the course carries no GT-Pathways designation, only the weak AACSB lock, and the catalog explicitly lets transfer students substitute it, so it is not hard prerequisite scaffolding. At 24 months a student could obtain much of this survey content from AI, but classroom delivery and assessment still anchor the instrumental need. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will deliver, tutor, and assess introductory business content on demand, and the learn-the-survey-from-an-instructor rationale weakens substantially. Because this course lacks the two brakes that hold comparable survey courses down (no general-education transfer mandate and no critical foundational-prerequisite status, given its explicit substitutability), little caps the erosion. Task-exposure research classifies this kind of informational, writing-adjacent knowledge work as highly exposed, and diffusion into education is already visible. The instrumental case shifts toward whatever the classroom adds beyond information transfer: structured context, discussion, and orientation for the major. That residue is real but thin for a survey course. The rating rises to High, hedged by the genuine possibility that curricular redesign re-centers the course on discussion and integration that AI delivers less well.

A decade out, AI is an authoritative, interactive business explainer, and the pure information-transmission purpose of an introductory survey is largely eroded. Without a GT mandate or a hard prerequisite role, nothing structural holds the instrumental case up; the only brake is the weak AACSB lock, which sets no course requirements. The central case has students able to acquire business literacy conversationally from capable models. The rating holds High. The honest uncertainty is not about capability, which is well within trajectory, but about whether the College of Business redesigns the course into an experiential, discussion-driven orientation whose value is the human cohort experience rather than content delivery. If it does, the instrumental case would be stronger than High implies; as currently described, a content survey, it is highly exposed.
BUS 1850.d: This course presents an introduction to business concepts that are further developed in the business core and in other courses pursued by business and economics majors. Also discussed are contemporary issues facing business. This course allows business students to develop a context for their studies and gives non-business students insights into the world of business. Transfer students that transfer in 6 or more credits of business courses may seek advisor approval to substitute BUS 1850 with another College of Business 3- credit hour course that does not appear in their Major or Business Core requirements.

r: The applied work spans business writing, listening, speaking, nonverbal and interpersonal communication with internal and external audiences, applied through written exercises and oral presentations. Mapped to O*NET, this is Communicating with Supervisors and Peers, Communicating with People Outside the Organization, and Performing for or Working Directly with the Public. The written component is highly exposed: controlled studies show large time savings and quality gains from AI writing assistance, and models draft business correspondence well. But a substantial part of the course is embodied: live oral presentation and real-time interpersonal and nonverbal communication, which task-exposure research places among low-exposure interpersonal categories, and which triggers a protective discount here. There is no licensure lock, only AACSB. At 24 months AI drafts the memos, but it does not develop the student's delivery and interpersonal presence. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI will draft, edit, and even rehearse-coach business communication, automating most of the written-production and preparation tasks. The instrumental case for the writing half erodes markedly. But the delivery and interpersonal half (presence, timing, reading an audience, nonverbal signaling, and responding live in a business setting) remains embodied and resistant, and the evidence on AI augmenting rather than substituting relational work supports that. No transfer mandate or accreditation requirement fixes the course in place, so the protection is structural to the task, not institutional. The rating rises to Medium: written execution automates and pushes exposure up, while the embodied delivery competence and the real-time interpersonal work keep it from High. The hedge is that if the course leans harder into automatable written artifacts, its exposure would climb.

A decade out, AI writes and edits business communication fluently and can rehearse spoken delivery, and the composition rationale is substantially eroded. But the core embodied competence, communicating persuasively and adaptively in real time with colleagues, clients, and audiences, is not a task AI performs on the speaker's behalf; embodiment and interpersonal presence keep it necessary. The rating holds Medium, lifted from Low by the now-automated writing component but held below High by the live-delivery and interpersonal core. The genuine uncertainty is how much of the course remains oral-and-interpersonal versus written: if business communication pedagogy migrates toward AI-mediated written artifacts, exposure rises; if it doubles down on live presentation and negotiation, the instrumental case strengthens. As described, the mix supports Medium.
BUS 1950.d: This marketing course explores multiple forms of communication within a business environment. Emphasis is placed on writing, listening, speaking, nonverbal and interpersonal communication with internal and external business audiences. Students apply the principles learned to written exercises and oral presentations.

r: The course is supervised, hands-on work experience in a real professional business environment, where the student examines how business disciplines operate in practice. The applied task is embodied workplace participation itself: showing up, contributing to real operations, and learning through situated presence. Mapped to O*NET this is Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships, Performing Administrative Activities in a live setting, and real-time Communicating with Peers. This is not a deliverable AI produces; it is experiential immersion, which task-exposure and observed-usage patterns place far outside automatable categories because it is physical, interpersonal, and real-time. No AI capability substitutes for a student personally gaining workplace experience. There is no institutional lock beyond AACSB, but none is needed; embodiment is the whole point. At 24 months the instrumental need is fully intact. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI tools will pervade the workplaces where interns are placed, changing what tasks interns are assigned and automating routine administrative work they might once have done. That reshapes the internship's content but not its instrumental purpose: the student still must personally inhabit a professional environment, build workplace relationships, and learn situated judgment that no model supplies on their behalf. The embodied, presence-based character of the experience is exactly what keeps it outside AI's reach, and the productivity evidence points to AI augmenting the surrounding work rather than replacing the human participant. No accreditation clock-hour mandate applies, but the experiential design is self-protecting. The rating stays Low, with the hedge that the mix of intern tasks shifts toward higher-order work as AI absorbs routine duties.

A decade out, workplaces will be heavily AI-mediated, and the routine tasks a first-year intern performs may be largely automated. Yet the instrumental core, a student acquiring real professional experience, relationships, and workplace acculturation through physical presence, is not something AI can do for the learner; it is categorically embodied and interpersonal. The rating holds Low with high confidence on the substitution question, distinct from any claim about the intern labor market, which is more exposed. The uncertainty is whether meaningful entry-level placements remain plentiful as AI absorbs junior work, an availability question rather than a substitutability one. On the rating's actual question, whether AI eliminates the need for a student to have the experience, the answer stays no.
BUS 1980.d: Internships provide practical, hands-on experience in a professional field related to business. Students will gain substantial work experience in a professional business environment where they will examine the role and importance of the different business disciplines in a real-world environment.

r: The applied work is a semester-long investigation of a single nonprofit culminating in a report that assesses the organization and recommends impact improvements. Mapped to O*NET this is Getting Information, Analyzing Data or Information, and Documenting/Recording Information, plus Provide Consultation and Advice to Others in report form. This research-analyze-write deliverable is precisely the kind of knowledge work AI performs well: GDPval finds frontier models approaching human-expert quality on real occupational deliverables, and writing-and-analysis tasks rank high in task-exposure research. A student could produce a competent organizational report with heavy AI assistance today. The protective factors are thin: no GT-Pathways designation, only the weak AACSB lock, and no hard prerequisite role. At 24 months the instrumental need is partly eroded but classroom framing and the applied learning process still anchor it. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will research an organization, synthesize public information, and draft an analytical report with improvement recommendations with facility, directly automating this course's central deliverable. GDPval-style capability and the strong task-exposure of writing and analysis both point upward, and diffusion into student workflows is already underway. Little structural protection remains (no transfer mandate, no licensure, no critical scaffolding), so the erosion is not capped the way general-education surveys are. The residual instrumental value is the student's own judgment about mission, impact, and stakeholder context, and the ability to verify AI-surfaced claims about an organization. The rating rises to High, hedged by the possibility that the course re-centers on field engagement with an actual nonprofit (interviews, site visits) which would restore embodied, harder-to-automate content.

A decade out, AI conducts organizational research and drafts impact analyses routinely, and the report-production rationale is largely eroded. The durable residue (evaluating a nonprofit's real-world impact, weighing stakeholder trade-offs, and verifying whether AI-generated recommendations are sound) remains a human competence, and the jagged-frontier evidence warns that plausible AI analysis can be wrong in non-obvious ways. But that residue is oversight, not production, and nothing institutional holds the course in place. The rating holds High. The honest uncertainty is pedagogical: if the course stays a research-and-report exercise it is highly exposed; if it becomes experiential nonprofit engagement, its instrumental case strengthens. As described, investigate and report, the deliverable sits inside AI's competent range.
BUS 2010.d: This survey course introduces the elements necessary for nonprofit organizations to achieve meaningful and lasting impact in their communities. Students will choose a single nonprofit to investigate throughout the semester, culminating in a report on the organization that includes suggestions for improving its impact.

r: This is a travel-based course: students research internationalization, then physically travel to a country to meet government and non-government agencies, local and international businesses, and experience the culture, integrating it into analysis of global business issues. The pre-travel research is exposed, but the defining applied work is embodied: international travel, in-person meetings, and cultural immersion. Mapped to O*NET this is Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships, Performing for or Working Directly with the Public, and situated Getting Information abroad. Task-exposure research places real-time interpersonal and physically situated activity firmly outside automatable categories, and no model substitutes for a student actually being in a foreign business environment. There is no licensure lock, but embodiment does the protective work decisively. At 24 months the instrumental need to have the physical, cross-cultural experience is untouched. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI will conduct the country and market research more thoroughly than any student pre-trip, and could simulate cultural briefings convincingly. That automates the analytical shell but not the course's reason for existing: physically meeting foreign officials and businesses and experiencing a culture firsthand is embodied and relational, exactly the activity that observed-usage and task-exposure evidence show AI does not perform. The integration of lived experience into business understanding requires the student to have been there. No accreditation mandate anchors the course, but its experiential design is self-protecting against substitution. The rating stays Low, with the hedge that AI increasingly displaces the desk-research component, shifting the course's instructional weight toward the in-country encounters that constitute its actual value.

A decade out, AI could offer richly immersive virtual simulations of foreign business environments, which is the strongest ten-year challenge to a travel course's premise. Even so, the central case distinguishes simulated exposure from the genuine embodied experience of traveling, meeting people, and navigating an unfamiliar culture in real time, the specific thing this course delivers and that AI does not perform for the student. The rating holds Low, anchored by embodiment and real-time interpersonal presence rather than any institutional lock. The honest uncertainty is whether institutions substitute cheaper virtual alternatives for physical travel, but that is a cost-and-format decision, not AI performing the experiential learning on the student's behalf. On substitutability, the experience remains the student's to have.
BUS 3010.d: This travel-based course focuses on the challenges and opportunities associated with entrepreneurship and various business strategies in the international business environment, including geography, culture, and economy of the country . Students first research an overview of the process and effects of internationalization in the current business environment, then travel to the country to meet with government and non-government agencies, local businesses, and international businesses, as well as experience aspects of local culture. Students integrate knowledge to identify the conceptual framework of global business issues and apply knowledge to business situations in a foreign country.

r: The course examines sustainable business through the integration of planet, people, and profits, using stakeholder analyses and case analyses and exploring values, cultural differences, and leadership. Mapped to O*NET the applied work is Analyzing Data or Information, Making Decisions and Solving Problems, and Documenting/Recording Information through written case and stakeholder analyses. These analytical-writing deliverables are exposed: task-exposure research ranks writing and analysis highly, and GDPval shows models approaching expert quality on real analytical deliverables. Ethical and cultural reasoning has a lower-exposure, critical-thinking dimension that tempers this somewhat, but the graded artifacts are largely writing. Protection is thin: no GT designation, only the weak AACSB lock, no prerequisite scaffolding role. At 24 months a student could produce competent CSR case analyses with substantial AI assistance, though classroom discussion still anchors the instrumental case. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI will draft stakeholder analyses, synthesize CSR cases, and generate sustainability assessments fluently, automating most of the course's written deliverables. The value-laden, cross-cultural, ethical-reasoning content is somewhat more resistant, as critical-thinking tasks are negatively associated with exposure in task-exposure research, but the assessment format is writing-heavy and thus exposed, and no institutional brake caps the erosion. The residual instrumental case is the student's own normative judgment about competing stakeholder claims and the ability to critically evaluate AI-generated sustainability reasoning. The rating rises to High, hedged meaningfully by the ethics-and-values core: if the course is taught and assessed as genuine moral and cross-cultural reasoning rather than report production, its exposure is lower than the rating suggests, which is why confidence here is not high.

A decade out, AI produces sophisticated CSR and sustainability analysis on demand, and the report-generation rationale is largely eroded. What endures is contested normative judgment, deciding what responsible business ought to do amid conflicting stakeholder values and cultural contexts, which is critical-reasoning work that task-exposure research treats as more durable, plus verifying whether AI's plausible ethical analysis is actually sound. But absent any institutional mandate, and given that the deliverables are written, the rating holds High. The honest uncertainty is larger than for a pure survey: the course's ethical and cross-cultural core is genuinely less automatable than its written artifacts, so if pedagogy centers the reasoning over the report, the instrumental case would be stronger than High implies.
BUS 3040.d: This course offers a global perspective of responsibility for conducting sustainable business. The over-arching theme is the integration of planet, people, and profits. Values and cultural differences among corporate entities, countries, and societies are explored within the context of stakeholder analyses. Leadership characteristics within successful companies are examined. Examples and case analyses provide means to explore social, cultural, and human aspects of doing business worldwide.

r: The course is supervised professional work experience, new to the student and overseen by a business professional, with faculty-guided reflection on approved learning objectives. The applied work is embodied workplace participation: performing real business tasks in a real organization and building situated judgment. Mapped to O*NET this is Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships, real-time Communicating with Peers and Supervisors, and Performing Administrative Activities in a live setting. This is experiential immersion, not a deliverable AI generates; task-exposure and observed-usage evidence place physically situated, interpersonal, real-time work outside automatable categories. No model substitutes for a student personally holding a supervised professional role. There is no clock-hour licensure mandate, only AACSB, but embodiment is self-protecting. At 24 months the instrumental need to gain real professional experience is fully intact. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI will be embedded in the host organizations, automating routine tasks an intern might perform and reshaping the intern's assignments toward oversight and higher-order work. That changes the internship's day-to-day content but not its instrumental purpose: the student must still occupy a professional role, form workplace relationships, and develop judgment through situated practice, none of which AI performs on the student's behalf. The productivity evidence supports augmentation of the surrounding work rather than replacement of the human participant. No accreditation clock-hour requirement fixes this course, but the experiential design protects it structurally. The rating stays Low, hedged by the acknowledgment that what interns actually do will shift substantially as AI absorbs routine business tasks.

A decade out, business workplaces will be pervasively AI-mediated and much junior work automated, raising a real question about the availability and content of meaningful internships. But the rating's question is substitutability of the learning experience, and that remains categorically embodied: a student gaining genuine professional experience, relationships, and workplace judgment is not work AI does for them. The rating holds Low. The genuine uncertainty concerns the entry-level labor market, whether substantive placements persist as AI absorbs junior tasks, which is an availability and economic question outside this rating. On whether AI eliminates the instrumental need for the student to have the experience itself, the answer stays no, anchored by embodiment and real-time interpersonal presence.
BUS 3980.d: Internships provide practical, hands-on experience in a professional field related to business. The internship must be based on work that is new to the student and supervised by a business professional. Internship placements must be approved through the internship credit approval process. Once enrolled, internship coursework is supervised by a faculty member. Students will complete academic work that encourages reflection regarding the approved learning objectives for the internship. Internship requirements vary by department. For information and instructions on finding and enrolling in an internship, contact the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub at [contact omitted].

r: The applied work is career self-management: industry research, self-assessment, occupational exploration, and preparation for employment, delivered experientially through observation, role-play, simulations, individual projects, and contact with resource experts. Mapped to O*NET this is Getting Information, Organizing and Planning work, and Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships. The research-and-materials tasks are exposed: observed-usage data shows writing and office tasks are prominent AI uses, and models handle occupational research and application preparation well. But the course's design is heavily interpersonal and experiential (role-play, simulations, live contact with resource experts) real-time activity task-exposure research places in low-exposure categories, which discounts the rating here. No licensure gates it, only AACSB. At 24 months AI assists the research and drafting, but not the student's experiential practice, self-assessment, and networking. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI career tools will conduct industry research, tailor application materials, and simulate interviews, automating much of the mechanical preparation the course covers. But the experiential and interpersonal spine (role-play, simulations, direct engagement with resource experts, and honest self-assessment) is embodied and relational, resisting substitution, and the evidence points to AI augmenting rather than replacing this kind of interpersonal work. No accreditation or licensure mandate holds the course in place; its protection is the real-time, personal nature of the competence itself. The rating stays Low, with the hedge that as AI absorbs the research-and-materials tasks, the course's instructional weight plausibly concentrates on the interviewing, networking, and self-reflection that models do not perform for the student.

A decade out, AI will manage nearly all mechanical career-preparation work (research, materials, scheduling, interview drills) and the honest question is whether a dedicated planning course still adds instrumental value. But the central case still requires the student to practice interpersonal professional interaction, engage real resource experts, and form a genuine self-assessment, tasks task-exposure research keeps outside AI's automatable range because they are interpersonal and self-referential. The rating holds Low, capped by the embodied, experiential design rather than any institutional mandate. The caveat is real: if the course collapsed to only the automatable research-and-application mechanics, its instrumental case would weaken beyond Low; as described, with role-play, simulations, and expert contact, the experiential core protects it.
BUS 4500.d: This course provides the opportunity for students to analyze and evaluate the information needed, processes involved, and the skills required for career planning. Processes of industry research, self-assessment, occupational exploration, and preparation for employment are critiqued, designed, and implemented. In addition to traditional classroom activities, content is presented in an experiential manner through observation, role-play, simulations, individual projects, and contact with resource experts.
